claim: Zebrafish skin has a superficial epidermis composed of ectoderm-derived epithelial cells.
source: Zebrafish skin, like all vertebrate skin, has a superficial epidermis composed of ectoderm-derived epithelial cells and an underlying dermis composed of mesoderm-derived mesenchymal cells and collagenous stromal matrix (Le Guellec et al., 2004; Aman and Parichy, 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Le Guellec et al., 2004; Aman and Parichy, 2020).

claim: Zebrafish skin has an underlying dermis composed of mesoderm-derived mesenchymal cells and collagenous stromal matrix.
source: Zebrafish skin, like all vertebrate skin, has a superficial epidermis composed of ectoderm-derived epithelial cells and an underlying dermis composed of mesoderm-derived mesenchymal cells and collagenous stromal matrix (Le Guellec et al., 2004; Aman and Parichy, 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Le Guellec et al., 2004; Aman and Parichy, 2020).

claim: During post-embryonic development, zebrafish skin simultaneously develops arrays of calcified scales and pigmented stripes.
source: During post-embryonic development, zebrafish skin simultaneously develops arrays of calcified scales and pigmented stripes.
evidence: Stated as a direct observation in the manuscript.

claim: Scales and pigmented stripes form superficially on the surface of the animal and are dispensable for survival in the laboratory.
source: Both form superficially on the surface of the animal and are dispensable for survival in the laboratory, making them readily amenable to imaging and experimental perturbation, and enabling analyses of underlying cellular dynamics and molecular mechanisms (Lee and Kimelman, 2002; Aman et al., 2018; Cox et al., 2018; Iwasaki et al., 2018; Rasmussen et al., 2018; Patterson and Parichy, 2019; Daane et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to published literature.

claim: Eda-Edar-NF-κB is a conserved signaling pathway necessary for normal skin appendage development in all vertebrates examined to date.
source: Eda-Edar-NF-κB is a conserved signaling pathway that is necessary for normal skin appendage development in all vertebrates examined to date (Kere et al., 1996; Srivastava et al., 1997; Kondo et al., 2001; Houghton et al., 2005; Harris et al., 2008; Di-Poï and Milinkovitch, 2016).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to published literature.

claim: Mutations in Eda-A, Edar, or downstream NF-κB pathway molecules underlie human ectodermal dysplasias.
source: Mutations in the signaling ligand Eda-A (Ectodysplasin-A), its receptor Edar, or downstream signal transduction molecules in the NF-κB (nuclear factor-κB) pathway underlie human ectodermal dysplasias, hereditary disorders defined by loss of skin appendages and teeth (Chu et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature (Chu et al., 2018).

claim: eda mutant zebrafish completely lack scales.
source: Similarly, eda mutant zebrafish completely lack scales, though specific mechanisms linking Eda signaling to scale formation remain unclear (Harris et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature (Harris et al., 2008).

claim: Bnc2 function is required in the hypodermis for survival and patterning of pigment cells.
source: Previous analysis of genetic mosaics demonstrated that Bnc2 function is required in the hypodermis for survival and patterning of pigment cells (Lang et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature (Lang et al., 2009).

claim: Thyroid hormone is necessary for dermal morphogenesis as well as pigment cell maturation and pattern formation.
source: We have shown that TH is necessary for dermal morphogenesis as well as pigment cell maturation and pattern formation though the underlying mechanisms remain elusive (McMenamin et al., 2014; Saunders et al., 2019; Aman et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (McMenamin et al., 2014; Saunders et al., 2019; Aman et al., 2021).

claim: At 9.2 SSL, wild-type zebrafish have all steps of scale development represented and are developing a pigment pattern of dark stripes alternating with light interstripes.
source: At 9.2 standardized standard length (SSL), approximately 3 wk post fertilization under standard conditions, wild-type zebrafish have all steps of scale development represented and are developing a pigment pattern of dark stripes, with melanophores and sparse iridophores, alternating with light interstripes of densely packed iridophores and yellow xanthophores.
evidence: Stated in text and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: Wild-type individuals of 9.6 SSL having precisely four rows of scales were selected for preparation of nuclei for sci-RNA-seq.
source: Wild-type individuals of 9.6 SSL having precisely four rows of scales were selected for preparation of nuclei to be used in single-cell indexed RNA-seq (sci-RNA-seq); eda mutants and hypoTH fish, devoid of scales, as well as bnc2 mutants having fewer, dysmorphic scales, were likewise reared to 9.6 SSL for isolation of nuclei.
evidence: Stated as a methodological detail in the manuscript.

claim: eda mutants and hypoTH fish are devoid of scales.
source: Wild-type individuals of 9.6 SSL having precisely four rows of scales were selected for preparation of nuclei to be used in single-cell indexed RNA-seq (sci-RNA-seq); eda mutants and hypoTH fish, devoid of scales, as well as bnc2 mutants having fewer, dysmorphic scales, were likewise reared to 9.6 SSL for isolation of nuclei.
evidence: Stated in text and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: bnc2 mutants have fewer, dysmorphic scales.
source: Wild-type individuals of 9.6 SSL having precisely four rows of scales were selected for preparation of nuclei to be used in single-cell indexed RNA-seq (sci-RNA-seq); eda mutants and hypoTH fish, devoid of scales, as well as bnc2 mutants having fewer, dysmorphic scales, were likewise reared to 9.6 SSL for isolation of nuclei.
evidence: Stated in text and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: High-quality transcriptomes were recovered from 144,466 individual nuclei with an average of 1300 UMIs and 720 genes detected per cell.
source: In total, we recovered high-quality transcriptomes from 144,466 individual nuclei with an average of 1300 unique molecular identifiers (UMIs) and 720 genes detected per cell (~60% duplication rate).
evidence: Stated as a result of the sci-RNA-seq experiment.

claim: Cell recovery, UMIs per cell, and numbers of genes detected were consistent across all sample groups.
source: Cell recovery, UMIs per cell, and numbers of genes detected were consistent across all sample groups (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Stated in text and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Likely multiplets (11%) were removed using Scrublet.
source: We removed likely multiplets (11%) using Scrublet (Wolock et al., 2019) and further processed the data and performed dimensionality reduction and clustering with monocle3 (Cao et al., 2019).
evidence: Stated as a methodological step with citation to the tool used.

claim: The majority of cells recovered were from epidermal and dermal populations.
source: The majority of cells were from epidermal and dermal populations, where we recovered transcripts from relatively rare subsets, including the edn3b/bnc2+ hypodermal monolayer that forms the deep limit of the dermis and shha+ epidermal placode cells at the posterior scale margin (Sire and Akimenko, 2004; Lang et al., 2009; Brock et al., 2019; Patterson and Parichy, 2013; Aman et al., 2018).
evidence: Stated as a result of the analysis with citations to support the identification of rare subsets.

claim: Transcripts from the edn3b/bnc2+ hypodermal monolayer that forms the deep limit of the dermis were recovered.
source: The majority of cells were from epidermal and dermal populations, where we recovered transcripts from relatively rare subsets, including the edn3b/bnc2+ hypodermal monolayer that forms the deep limit of the dermis and shha+ epidermal placode cells at the posterior scale margin (Sire and Akimenko, 2004; Lang et al., 2009; Brock et al., 2019; Patterson and Parichy, 2013; Aman et al., 2018).
evidence: Stated as a result of the analysis with citations to support the identification.

claim: Transcripts from shha+ epidermal placode cells at the posterior scale margin were recovered.
source: The majority of cells were from epidermal and dermal populations, where we recovered transcripts from relatively rare subsets, including the edn3b/bnc2+ hypodermal monolayer that forms the deep limit of the dermis and shha+ epidermal placode cells at the posterior scale margin (Sire and Akimenko, 2004; Lang et al., 2009; Brock et al., 2019; Patterson and Parichy, 2013; Aman et al., 2018).
evidence: Stated as a result of the analysis with citations to support the identification.

claim: Dermal scale forming cells (SFCs) and their progenitors (pre-SFCs) were recovered.
source: As expected, based on our stage selection, we recovered dermal scale forming cells (SFCs) and their progenitors (pre-SFCs) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Stated as a result of the analysis and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Less abundant cell types including pigment cells, lateral line cells, goblet cells, ionocytes, glia, and immune cells were recovered.
source: We also recovered less abundant cell types, including pigment cells, lateral line cells, goblet cells, ionocytes, glia, and immune cells (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Stated as a result of the analysis and shown in figures.

claim: Adult zebrafish are adorned with a full coat of partially overlapping elasmoid scales.
source: Adult zebrafish are adorned with a full coat of partially overlapping elasmoid scales, thin plates of calcified ECM that grow between the dermis and epidermis during post-embryonic development (Figure 1, Figure 1—figure supplement 1; Sire et al., 1997a; Aman et al., 2018).
evidence: Stated in text with citations and shown in figures.

claim: Elasmoid scales are thin plates of calcified ECM that grow between the dermis and epidermis during post-embryonic development.
source: Adult zebrafish are adorned with a full coat of partially overlapping elasmoid scales, thin plates of calcified ECM that grow between the dermis and epidermis during post-embryonic development (Figure 1, Figure 1—figure supplement 1; Sire et al., 1997a; Aman et al., 2018).
evidence: Stated in text with citations to published literature.

claim: Scale development is associated with a population of dermal cells that express sp7 and runx2a/b.
source: Scale development is associated with a population of dermal cells—referred to here as SFCs—that express genes encoding transcription factors, including sp7 (also known as osterix, osx) and runx2a/b, that are necessary for differentiation of osteoblasts and odontoblasts (Sire et al., 1997a; Komori, 2010; Li et al., 2011a; Zhang, 2012; Aman et al., 2018; Bae et al., 2018; Cox et al., 2018; Iwasaki et al., 2018; Rasmussen et al., 2018).
evidence: Stated in text with citations to published literature.

claim: sp7 and runx2a/b are necessary for differentiation of osteoblasts and odontoblasts.
source: Scale development is associated with a population of dermal cells—referred to here as SFCs—that express genes encoding transcription factors, including sp7 (also known as osterix, osx) and runx2a/b, that are necessary for differentiation of osteoblasts and odontoblasts (Sire et al., 1997a; Komori, 2010; Li et al., 2011a; Zhang, 2012; Aman et al., 2018; Bae et al., 2018; Cox et al., 2018; Iwasaki et al., 2018; Rasmussen et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Basal epidermal cells give rise to both suprabasal cells and periderm cells.
source: Scale development also coincides with expansion of the three major epidermal cell types—periderm (also known as superficial epidermal cells), suprabasal cells, and basal cells—of which basal cells give rise to both of the other cell types (Lee et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature (Lee et al., 2014).

claim: Transcriptomic analyses confirmed that SFCs express sp7 and likely differentiate from runx2b+ progenitors.
source: Our transcriptomic analyses confirmed that SFCs express sp7 and suggested that they likely differentiate from runx2b+ progenitors (Figure 2A).
evidence: Stated as a result of transcriptomic analysis and shown in Figure 2A.

claim: runx2b is consistently more broadly expressed than sp7 during scale development.
source: Comparing runx2b and sp7 mRNA distributions during scale development revealed that runx2b is consistently more broadly expressed than sp7, suggesting the existence of a restricted halo of SFC progenitors surrounding the growing scale (Figure 2B and D).
evidence: Stated as a result of comparing mRNA distributions and shown in Figure 2B and D.

claim: A restricted halo of SFC progenitors surrounds the growing scale.
source: Comparing runx2b and sp7 mRNA distributions during scale development revealed that runx2b is consistently more broadly expressed than sp7, suggesting the existence of a restricted halo of SFC progenitors surrounding the growing scale (Figure 2B and D).
evidence: Inferred from the broader expression of runx2b compared to sp7 and shown in Figure 2B and D.

claim: Over 3 days of scale development, numerous cells acquire nuclear nEOS expression as they are incorporated into growing scales.
source: As expected, over 3 d of scale development, we observed numerous cells acquire nuclear nEOS expression as they were incorporated into growing scales, supporting the inference that peripheral, presumptively runx2b+ dermal cells differentiate as SFCs (Figure 2C and D).
evidence: Stated as a result of live imaging experiments and shown in Figure 2C and D.

claim: Peripheral, presumptively runx2b+ dermal cells differentiate as SFCs.
source: As expected, over 3 d of scale development, we observed numerous cells acquire nuclear nEOS expression as they were incorporated into growing scales, supporting the inference that peripheral, presumptively runx2b+ dermal cells differentiate as SFCs (Figure 2C and D).
evidence: Inferred from the observation that cells acquire nEOS expression as they are incorporated into scales and shown in Figure 2C and D.

claim: SFCs at the posterior margin are progressively displaced towards the scale focus by addition of newly differentiated SFCs from sp7-negative progenitors.
source: These analyses showed that SFCs at the posterior margin are progressively displaced towards the scale focus, presumably by addition of newly differentiated SFCs from sp7-negative progenitors (Figure 2E, top).
evidence: Stated as a result of photoconversion experiments and shown in Figure 2E.

claim: SFCs in the sub-marginal region contribute to elongated marginal cells, scale radii cells, and an SFC subset that rapidly displaces toward the scale focus.
source: SFCs in the sub-marginal region contributed to elongated marginal cells, scale radii cells, and an SFC subset that rapidly displaced toward the scale focus (Figure 2E, middle).
evidence: Stated as a result of photoconversion experiments and shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Cells at the focus in a nascent scale remain in the focus as the scale grows.
source: Lastly, cells at the focus in a nascent scale remained in the focus as the scale grew (Figure 2E, bottom).
evidence: Stated as a result of photoconversion experiments and shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Radii cells descend from marginal SFCs.
source: These results demonstrate that radii cells descend from marginal SFCs, consistent with previous live imaging results (Cox et al., 2018; Iwasaki et al., 2018; Rasmussen et al., 2018), confirming that SFCs do not pass through an intermediate state as scale radii cells during differentiation, which a facile interpretation of pseudotemporal ordering might suggest.
evidence: Stated as a result of the experiments with citations to previous studies.

claim: SFCs do not pass through an intermediate state as scale radii cells during differentiation.
source: These results demonstrate that radii cells descend from marginal SFCs, consistent with previous live imaging results (Cox et al., 2018; Iwasaki et al., 2018; Rasmussen et al., 2018), confirming that SFCs do not pass through an intermediate state as scale radii cells during differentiation, which a facile interpretation of pseudotemporal ordering might suggest.
evidence: Stated as a conclusion from the experiments.

claim: Pseudotemporal ordering did not faithfully represent the cell state path during SFC differentiation.
source: Thus, although cell state transitions inferred from transcriptomes alone can suggest cell lineage relationships and cell states along a differentiation continuum, we find that the pseudotemporal ordering, while continuous from pre-SFC to differentiated SFC, did not faithfully represent the cell state path during SFC differentiation.
evidence: Stated as a conclusion from comparing pseudotemporal ordering with live imaging results.

claim: The continuity of cell states revealed by pseudotemporal ordering could reflect continuous variation in other biological processes apart from differentiation, like states of the cell cycle or migration.
source: Instead, the continuity of cell states revealed by pseudotemporal ordering could reflect continuous variation in other biological processes apart from differentiation, like states of the cell cycle or migration (Haghverdi et al., 2015; Saunders et al., 2019).
evidence: Stated as an interpretation with citations to support the idea.

claim: Pseudotemporal order in the SFC dataset might reflect differences in gene expression associated with mesenchymal and epithelial states.
source: Given the mesenchymal appearance of pre-SFC dermal cells and the epithelial appearance of differentiated SFCs (Figure 2C; Figure 1—figure supplement 1) (Iwasaki et al., 2018; Aman et al., 2021), we predicted that pseudotemporal order in this dataset might reflect differences in gene expression associated with these different cellular morphologies.
evidence: Stated as a prediction based on observations and citations.

claim: The ratio of epithelial-to-mesenchymal scores corresponds with pseudotemporal order in SFCs.
source: To test this possibility, we constructed gene expression signatures for mesenchymal and epithelial states from the literature and mapped the ratio of epithelial-to-mesenchymal scores on cells in UMAP space, which revealed an overall correspondence of these scores with pseudotemporal order (Figure 2F and G).
evidence: Stated as a result of testing the prediction and shown in Figure 2F and G.

claim: Differentiated SFCs remain proliferative.
source: Finally, our observations also provided an opportunity to resolve a controversy as to whether differentiated SFCs are capable of proliferating or whether scale growth occurs exclusively by hypertrophic growth of individual cells (Cox et al., 2018; Iwasaki et al., 2018): both transcriptomic analyses and live imaging experiments showed that differentiated SFCs remain proliferative (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B–D).
evidence: Stated as a result of transcriptomic and live imaging analyses and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2B–D.

claim: During post-embryonic skin maturation, basal epidermal cells are the stem cell population that differentiate into both suprabasal and periderm cells.
source: During this stage of development, basal epidermal cells are the stem cell population that differentiate into both suprabasal and periderm cells, and each of the three major epidermal cell types are well represented in our dataset (Figure 2H and I, Figure 1—figure supplement 3; Guzman et al., 2013; Lee et al., 2014).
evidence: Stated in text with citations and shown in figures.

claim: Suprabasal cells are entirely derived from basal cells.
source: While periderm cells at the sampled stage are likely of dual origin, representing a mixture of early embryonic and stem cell-derived cells, suprabasal cells are entirely derived from basal cells (Kimmel et al., 1990; Guzman et al., 2013; Lee et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The trajectories between basal cells, suprabasal cells, and periderm were discontinuous in UMAP space.
source: While the established cell type markers for basal cells and periderm cells, tp63 and krt4, displayed a clear transition between basal cells (tp63+, krt4-), suprabasal cells (tp63+, krt4+), and periderm (tp63-, krt4+), the trajectories were discontinuous in UMAP space (Figure 2I and J).
evidence: Stated as a result of the analysis and shown in Figure 2I and J.

claim: Discontinuities among epidermal cell subtypes reflect abrupt transcriptional changes during differentiation.
source: Moreover, the number of differentially expressed genes between each of the epidermal types was about twice as large as between cell clusters having continuous trajectories (basal cell vs. periderm, 7341 DEGs; basal cell vs. suprabasal, 4024 DEGs; pre-SFC vs. SFC, 2373 DEGs; all q < 0.01), suggesting that discontinuities among epidermal cell subtypes reflect abrupt transcriptional changes during differentiation, rather than artifacts of the dimensionality reduction itself.
evidence: Inferred from the number of differentially expressed genes between cell types.

claim: Calcified skin appendages are an ancient vertebrate trait first appearing in the Ordovician 450 million years ago.
source: Calcified skin appendages are an ancient vertebrate trait with a robust fossil record, first appearing in the Ordovician 450 million years ago, prior to the appearance of paired fins, jaws, and teeth (Smith et al., 2002; Märss, 2006; Sire et al., 2009; Fraser et al., 2010; Turner et al., 2010; Janvier, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Ancestral skin appendages were morphologically and compositionally similar to modern-day teeth.
source: These ancestral skin appendages were morphologically and compositionally similar to modern-day teeth, with a hypercalcified, enamel-like matrix capping collagen-rich calcified matrices resembling dentin, bone, or both (Quan et al., 2020; Smith et al., 2002; Märss, 2006; Sire et al., 2009; Figure 3A).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature and shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The flattened morphology and elastic flexibility of elasmoid scales typical of most extant fish are highly derived.
source: While certain extant non-teleost fishes, like sharks, bichir, and gar, have scales that resemble skin appendages of ancient fishes and modern teeth, the flattened morphology and elastic flexibility of elasmoid scales typical of most extant fish are highly derived (Quan et al., 2020; Sire et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Elasmoid scales of zebrafish are composed of weakly calcified collagenous matrix known as elasmoidin, capped by a collagen-free, hypermineralized limiting layer.
source: Histological and ultrastructural studies have shown that the elasmoid scales of zebrafish and other teleosts are composed of weakly calcified collagenous matrix, known as elasmoidin, capped by a collagen-free, hypermineralized limiting layer that forms in close proximity to basal epidermal cells with an overtly secretory morphology (Figure 3A; Quan et al., 2020; Sire et al., 1997b; Quan et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature and shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The hypermineralized limiting layer of elasmoid scales forms in close proximity to basal epidermal cells with an overtly secretory morphology.
source: Histological and ultrastructural studies have shown that the elasmoid scales of zebrafish and other teleosts are composed of weakly calcified collagenous matrix, known as elasmoidin, capped by a collagen-free, hypermineralized limiting layer that forms in close proximity to basal epidermal cells with an overtly secretory morphology (Figure 3A; Quan et al., 2020; Sire et al., 1997b; Quan et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature.

claim: A transcriptionally distinct population of basal epidermal cells expresses EMP genes.
source: Consistent with our prediction, we identified a transcriptionally distinct population of basal epidermal cells, separated from other basal epidermal cells in UMAP projections, that expressed EMP genes (Figure 3B and C).
evidence: Stated as a result of the analysis and shown in Figure 3B and C.

claim: Transcripts of the conserved EMP gene ambn were found almost exclusively in EMP+ epidermal cells.
source: Strikingly, transcripts of the conserved EMP gene ambn were found almost exclusively in this subpopulation of basal cells, which we refer to as EMP+ epidermal cells (Figure 3B and C).
evidence: Stated as a result of the analysis and shown in Figure 3B and C.

claim: EMP+ epidermal cells are positioned precisely where epidermal cells contact the scale matrix.
source: To test correspondence of that population with EMP+ epidermal cells identified in our transcriptomic data, we visualized ambn expression by in situ mRNA hybridization, which revealed that EMP+ epidermal cells are positioned precisely where epidermal cells contact the scale matrix (Figure 3D–F).
evidence: Stated as a result of in situ hybridization and shown in Figure 3D–F.

claim: EMP+ epidermal cells express dlx3a, dlx4a, msx2a, and runx2b, transcription factors that regulate mammalian ameloblast differentiation.
source: Indeed, we find that dlx3a, dlx4a, msx2a, and runx2b are expressed in these cells (Figure 3B; Pemberton et al., 2007; Debiais-Thibaud et al., 2011; Urzúa et al., 2011; Bae et al., 2018; Chu et al., 2018; Woodruff et al., 2022; Li et al., 2011b).
evidence: Stated as a result of the analysis with citations and shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The enamel-like, hypermineralized limiting layer of the scale is produced by deeply conserved, ameloblast-like epidermal cells.
source: Together, these results suggest that the enamel-like, hypermineralized limiting layer of the scale is produced by deeply conserved, ameloblast-like epidermal cells.
evidence: Inferred from the expression of EMP genes and ameloblast-associated transcription factors in epidermal cells.

claim: Dermal SFCs express transcripts of Osteopontin (spp1) and Chondroadherin (chad), encoding bone matrix proteins.
source: Consistent with an overall similarity between osteoblasts and SFCs, we detected transcripts of Osteopontin (spp1) (Figure 3B and I) and Chondroadherin (chad) (Figure 3B and I, Figure 2—figure supplement 1J), encoding bone matrix proteins, in addition to Secretory-calcium-binding Phosphoprotein 1 (scpp1), which is homologous to human Dentin-Matrix-Acidic Proteins that form a component of both bone and dentin (Figure 3B and I; Larsson et al., 1991; Raouf et al., 2002; Hessle et al., 2013; Venkatesh et al., 2014; Braasch et al., 2016; Kawasaki et al., 2017).
evidence: Stated as a result of the analysis with citations and shown in figures.

claim: Dermal SFCs express transcripts of Secretory-calcium-binding Phosphoprotein 1 (scpp1), homologous to human Dentin-Matrix-Acidic Proteins.
source: Consistent with an overall similarity between osteoblasts and SFCs, we detected transcripts of Osteopontin (spp1) (Figure 3B and I) and Chondroadherin (chad) (Figure 3B and I, Figure 2—figure supplement 1J), encoding bone matrix proteins, in addition to Secretory-calcium-binding Phosphoprotein 1 (scpp1), which is homologous to human Dentin-Matrix-Acidic Proteins that form a component of both bone and dentin (Figure 3B and I; Larsson et al., 1991; Raouf et al., 2002; Hessle et al., 2013; Venkatesh et al., 2014; Braasch et al., 2016; Kawasaki et al., 2017).
evidence: Stated as a result of the analysis with citations and shown in figures.

claim: Robust expression of transcripts encoding bone matrix proteins Osteocrin (ostn) or Osteocalcin (bglap) was not detected in SFCs.
source: Nevertheless, we failed to detect robust expression of transcripts encoding bone matrix proteins Osteocrin (ostn) or Osteocalcin (bone gamma-carboxyglutamate protein [bglap]) in SFCs (Figure 3B; Thomas et al., 2003).
evidence: Stated as a result of the analysis with citation and shown in Figure 3B.

claim: SFCs express EMP genes and genes encoding fish-specific SCPPs.
source: In addition to a subset of bone-specific transcripts, SFCs also expressed EMP genes and genes encoding fish-specific SCPPs (Figure 3B and I).
evidence: Stated as a result of the analysis and shown in Figure 3B and I.

claim: The bone-associated transcripts spp1 and chad are primarily expressed in the scale focus and radii SFCs.
source: Expression was spatially restricted among SFCs, with the bone-associated transcripts, spp1 and chad, primarily expressed in the scale focus and radii SFCs, while EMP genes were restricted to SFCs at the scale margin (Figure 3B, G, H and I, Figure 2—figure supplement 1J).
evidence: Stated as a result of the analysis and shown in figures.

claim: EMP genes are restricted to SFCs at the scale margin.
source: Expression was spatially restricted among SFCs, with the bone-associated transcripts, spp1 and chad, primarily expressed in the scale focus and radii SFCs, while EMP genes were restricted to SFCs at the scale margin (Figure 3B, G, H and I, Figure 2—figure supplement 1J).
evidence: Stated as a result of the analysis and shown in figures.

claim: Dermal SFCs express col10a1a and col10a1b transcripts.
source: The zebrafish genome harbors genes encoding two Col10a1 orthologs (col10a1a and col10a1b), and we found both transcripts in SFCs representing distinct steps of maturation; however, transcripts of Col2a1 genes (col2a1a and col2a1b) were not robustly detected in these cells (Figure 3B and I, Figure 2—figure supplement 1F and I).
evidence: Stated as a result of the analysis and shown in figures.

claim: Transcripts of Col2a1 genes (col2a1a and col2a1b) were not robustly detected in SFCs.
source: The zebrafish genome harbors genes encoding two Col10a1 orthologs (col10a1a and col10a1b), and we found both transcripts in SFCs representing distinct steps of maturation; however, transcripts of Col2a1 genes (col2a1a and col2a1b) were not robustly detected in these cells (Figure 3B and I, Figure 2—figure supplement 1F and I).
evidence: Stated as a result of the analysis and shown in figures.

claim: Both eda mutants and hypoTH fish completely lack scales at the stage sampled.
source: Both eda mutants and hypoTH fish completely lack scales at the stage sampled, allowing us to compare transcriptomic signatures and cell type complements associated with scale loss in these different backgrounds (Figure 1A).
evidence: Stated in text and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Both scale-free conditions were characterized by a complete lack of fully differentiated dermal SFCs.
source: Analyses of cell type abundance revealed that both scale-free conditions were characterized by a complete lack of fully differentiated dermal SFCs (Figure 4A and B).
evidence: Stated as a result of the analysis and shown in Figure 4A and B.

claim: eda mutants retained a small subset of dermal pre-SFC progenitors.
source: These analyses further showed that eda mutants—despite homozygosity for a presumptive null allele—retained a small subset of dermal pre-SFC progenitors, whereas hypoTH skins lacked pre-SFC entirely.
evidence: Stated as a result of the analysis.

claim: hypoTH skins lacked pre-SFC entirely.
source: These analyses further showed that eda mutants—despite homozygosity for a presumptive null allele—retained a small subset of dermal pre-SFC progenitors, whereas hypoTH skins lacked pre-SFC entirely.
evidence: Stated as a result of the analysis.

claim: hypoTH fish lack superficial dermal cell types at the stage sampled for sequencing.
source: We have previously shown that hypoTH fish lack superficial dermal cell types at the stage sampled for sequencing, though these cell types do appear later in development (Aman et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study (Aman et al., 2021).

claim: eda mutants exhibit a population of ET37:EGFP+ dermal cells beneath the epidermis that is not present in hypoTH fish.
source: Indeed, eda mutants exhibited a population of ET37:EGFP+ dermal cells—presumptive pre-SFC—beneath the epidermis that was not present in hypoTH fish (Figure 4C and D).
evidence: Stated as a result of live imaging and shown in Figure 4C and D.

claim: Eda-Edar-NF-κB signals are transmitted from the dermis to epidermis during scale morphogenesis.
source: In previous work, we found that Eda-Edar-NF-κB signals are transmitted from the dermis to epidermis during scale morphogenesis (Aman et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study (Aman et al., 2018).

claim: edar is expressed in the epidermis during scale morphogenesis.
source: The signaling ligand, encoded by eda, has a dynamic expression pattern that shifts from broad expression in unspecified epidermis to localized expression in dermal papillae during scale morphogenesis. These expression dynamics are strikingly similar during mouse hair follicle and chicken feather patterning (Montonen et al., 1998; Harris et al., 2008; Houghton et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature.

claim: eda has a dynamic expression pattern that shifts from broad expression in unspecified epidermis to localized expression in dermal papillae during scale morphogenesis.
source: The signaling ligand, encoded by eda, has a dynamic expression pattern that shifts from broad expression in unspecified epidermis to localized expression in dermal papillae during scale morphogenesis.
evidence: Stated as a known expression pattern.

claim: edar is detected primarily in basal epidermal cells, with most intense expression in the shha+ epidermal placode.
source: We confirmed that these expression domains were reflected in our sci-RNA-seq data, in which edar is detected primarily in basal epidermal cells, with most intense expression in the shha+ epidermal placode (Figure 5A; Aman et al., 2018).
evidence: Stated as a result of the analysis with citation and shown in Figure 5A.

claim: eda transcripts were detected at much lower levels and were much more dispersed across cell types than edar transcripts but were enriched in pre-SFC.
source: eda transcripts were detected at much lower levels and were much more dispersed across cell types than edar transcripts but were nevertheless enriched in pre-SFC as expected (Figure 5A).
evidence: Stated as a result of the analysis and shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Epidermal expression of Fgf ligands is Eda-dependent.
source: Our transcriptomic analysis showed that, indeed, epidermal expression of Fgf ligands is Eda-dependent (Figure 5B and C).
evidence: Stated as a result of the analysis and shown in Figure 5B and C.

claim: fgf20a plays a conserved role in regulating dermal morphogenesis in amniote skin appendage development.
source: Among Fgf ligand transcripts detected in epidermis was that of fgf20a, which plays a conserved role in regulating dermal morphogenesis in amniote skin appendage development and has been implicated in scale development and regeneration in zebrafish (Huh et al., 2013; Daane et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Heatshock-driven expression of Fgf20a in basal epidermal cells of Eda mutants led to localized rescue of scales.
source: Indeed, heatshock-driven expression in F0 mosaics stringently selected for basal epidermal expression of Fgf20a in the skin of Eda mutants led to localized rescue of scales where transgene expression was detectable (Figure 5D).
evidence: Stated as a result of the experiment and shown in Figure 5D.

claim: fgf20a mutant zebrafish do not have a squamation phenotype unless present in an fgfr1a mutant background.
source: Notably, fgf20a mutant zebrafish do not have a squamation phenotype unless present in an fgfr1a mutant background, suggesting functional redundancy among Fgf ligands (Daane et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature (Daane et al., 2016).

claim: Eda-Edar-NF-κB signaling regulates SFC differentiation via multiple epidermal Fgf ligands, including Fgf20a.
source: Those results and our present findings together suggest that Eda-Edar-NF-κB signaling regulates SFC differentiation via multiple epidermal Fgf ligands, including Fgf20a.
evidence: Inferred from the results of the experiments and previous findings.

claim: Substantial differences in gene expression between wild-type and hypoTH backgrounds were found in dermal and epidermal cell types, particularly in basal cells of the epidermis.
source: This analysis revealed substantial differences in gene expression between backgrounds in dermal and epidermal cell types, and particularly in basal cells of the epidermis (Figure 6A).
evidence: Stated as a result of the analysis and shown in Figure 6A.

claim: TH regulates the expression of cues in epidermal basal cells that recruit dermal cells to the most superficial layer of the dermis prior to scale papilla formation.
source: Given the absence of superficial pre-SFC in hypoTH skin (Figure 4B–D), we hypothesized that TH regulates the expression of cues in epidermal basal cells that recruit dermal cells to the most superficial layer of the dermis, subjacent to the epidermis, prior to scale papilla formation (Aman et al., 2021).
evidence: Stated as a hypothesis based on observations with citation.

claim: Markedly reduced expression of several non-FGF MAPK ligand genes, including PDGFα orthologs (pdgfaa, pdgfab), was found between wild-type and hypoTH basal cells.
source: To test this idea, we examined ligand genes with detectable expression across each of the seven major pathways between wild-type and hypoTH basal cells, which revealed markedly reduced expression for several non-FGF MAPK ligand genes, including PDGFα orthologs (pdgfaa, pdgfab) that are known in amniotes to regulate mesenchymal cell motility and proliferation (Figure 6B–D; Karlsson et al., 1999).
evidence: Stated as a result of the analysis with citation and shown in Figure 6B–D.

claim: PDGFα orthologs (pdgfaa, pdgfab) are known in amniotes to regulate mesenchymal cell motility and proliferation.
source: To test this idea, we examined ligand genes with detectable expression across each of the seven major pathways between wild-type and hypoTH basal cells, which revealed markedly reduced expression for several non-FGF MAPK ligand genes, including PDGFα orthologs (pdgfaa, pdgfab) that are known in amniotes to regulate mesenchymal cell motility and proliferation (Figure 6B–D; Karlsson et al., 1999).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature (Karlsson et al., 1999).

claim: Forced expression of Pdgfaa in basal cells of the epidermis in hypoTH fish rescued the formation of superficial dermal cells.
source: When we forced expression of Pdgfaa in basal cells of epidermis by heatshock induction and stringent selection of basal epidermal expression in F0 mosaics, we found, as predicted, a recruitment of dermal cells in hypoTH skin, leading to a locally stratified dermis (Figure 6E) similar to that of the wild-type (Figure 4C).
evidence: Stated as a result of the experiment and shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Early, heatshock-induced Pdgfaa expression led to precocious dermal stratification in wild-type and eda mutant fish.
source: Early, heatshock-induced Pdgfaa expression also led to precocious dermal stratification in wild-type and eda mutant fish (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Stated as a result of the experiment and shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Pdgfaa expression did not rescue the onset of squamation in hypoTH fish.
source: Pdgfaa expression did not, however, rescue the onset of squamation in hypoTH fish, which begins at a larger size and only after about twice the time as in wild-type fish (14 SSL vs. 9 SSL, 40 vs. 21 d post-fertilization in our rearing conditions) (Aman et al., 2021).
evidence: Stated as a result of the experiment with citation.

claim: Pdgfaa did not lead to mis-patterned and dysmorphic scales in wild-type fish, or a rescue of squamation in eda mutants.
source: Nor did Pdgfaa lead to mis-patterned and dysmorphic scales in wild-type fish, or a rescue of squamation in eda mutants, as we observed for Fgf20a (Figure 5D).
evidence: Stated as a result of the experiment.

claim: Pdgfaa-dependent stratification of dermis and Fgf-dependent differentiation of SFC are functionally decoupled processes that occur sequentially during skin morphogenesis.
source: Together, these observations suggest that Pdgfaa-dependent stratification of dermis and Fgf-dependent differentiation of SFC are functionally decoupled processes that occur sequentially during skin morphogenesis (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Inferred from the results of the experiments and shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Additional TH transcriptional targets regulate skin morphogenesis.
source: Because Pdgfaa rescued dermis stratification, but not scale development in hypoTH skin, we predict that additional TH transcriptional targets regulate skin morphogenesis.
evidence: Stated as a prediction based on the experimental results.

claim: At 9.6 SSL, bonaparte mutants have fewer iridophores and melanophores compared to wild-type controls.
source: At the stage of tissue collection, fewer iridophores and melanophores were evident in bnc2 mutants compared to wild-type controls, mirroring prior quantitative comparisons (Figure 8A).
evidence: Stated as an observation and shown in Figure 8A.

claim: Wild-type and bnc2 mutant fish have a profound deficiency of hypodermal cells.
source: Yet alignment of UMAP projections for wild-type and bnc2 mutant cells revealed instead a profound deficiency of hypodermal cells themselves (Figure 8B).
evidence: Stated as a result of the analysis and shown in Figure 8B.

claim: Marked deficits in hypodermal cells, iridophores, melanophores, and xanthophores were found in bnc2 mutants, whereas the numbers of dermal mesenchyme cells were relatively unchanged.
source: We quantified the proportion of various dermal cell types and pigment cells relative to wild-type controls in our sci-RNA-seq dataset and found marked deficits in hypodermal cells, as well as iridophores, melanophores, and xanthophores, whereas the numbers of dermal mesenchyme cells were relatively unchanged between genotypes (Figure 7C).
evidence: Stated as a result of the analysis and shown in Figure 7C (note: this should be Figure 8C based on context).

claim: Stage-matched bnc2 mutant dermis had dermal mesenchyme, but lacked a hypodermal layer.
source: In wild-type controls, the hypodermis appeared as a thin, nearly confluent cell layer deep in the dermis, whereas in bnc2 mutants no such layer was apparent; instead, the deepest dermis appeared to contain only dermal mesenchyme (Figure 8D, Figure 8—figure supplement 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Stated as a result of live imaging and shown in Figure 8D.

claim: Iridophores and melanophores are in close proximity to ET37:EGFP+ hypodermal cells in wild-type skin.
source: Consistent with the hypodermis having roles in supporting pigment cells, we observed iridophores, expressing pnp4a:palm-mCherry and melanophores, expressing tyrp1b:palm-mCherry in close proximity to ET37:EGFP+ hypodermal cells in wild-type skin (Figure 8E; McMenamin et al., 2014; Lewis et al., 2019).
evidence: Stated as an observation with citations and shown in Figure 8E.

claim: Hypodermal cells are the principal cells to express endothelin 3b (edn3b).
source: These analyses revealed that hypodermal cells are likely to be an important driver of iridophore development as they were the principal cells to express endothelin 3b (edn3b) (Figure 8F, Figure 8—figure supplement 1B), encoding a secreted protein that is processed to an active 21 amino acid peptide required by iridophores.
evidence: Stated as a result of the analysis and shown in Figure 8F.

claim: Diminished expression of edn3b is associated with reduced numbers of iridophores and attenuated interstripes and stripes in zebrafish mutants and Danio nigrofasciatus.
source: Diminished expression of edn3b is associated with reduced numbers of iridophores and attenuated interstripes and stripes both in zebrafish mutants and in the naturally occurring pattern of the zebrafish relative, Danio nigrofasciatus (Spiewak et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature (Spiewak et al., 2018).

claim: Edn3 acts directly on iridophores but only indirectly on melanophores through an interaction between these cells and Edn3-dependent iridophores.
source: Edn3 acts directly on iridophores but only indirectly on melanophores through an interaction between these cells and Edn3-dependent iridophores (Parichy et al., 2000; Krauss et al., 2014; Spiewak et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Hypodermal cells express agouti signaling protein 1 (asip1), which encodes a secreted protein that represses melanophore differentiation in ventral regions of the flank.
source: More direct roles for hypodermal cells in regulating melanophore development were suggested by expression of other factors, including agouti signaling protein 1 (asip1), which encodes a secreted protein that represses melanophore differentiation in ventral regions of the flank (Cal et al., 2019), though our dataset does not allow us to segment cells spatially.
evidence: Stated as a result of the analysis with citation.

claim: kitlga was expressed at higher levels by melanophores themselves.
source: Interestingly, kit ligand a (kitlga), encoding a melanogenic factor that promotes survival, migration, and differentiation, was expressed at only moderate levels by hypodermal cells at this stage, despite its broad expression in the much simpler skin of embryos and early larvae (Hultman et al., 2007; Brock et al., 2019; Dooley et al., 2013). Nevertheless, kitlga was expressed at higher levels by melanophores themselves, whereas junctional adhesion molecule 3b (jam3b), encoding a 2-immunoglobulin-like domain adhesion receptor, was expressed by both hypodermal cells and melanophores.
evidence: Stated as a result of the analysis with citations.

claim: junctional adhesion molecule 3b (jam3b) was expressed by both hypodermal cells and melanophores.
source: Nevertheless, kitlga was expressed at higher levels by melanophores themselves, whereas junctional adhesion molecule 3b (jam3b), encoding a 2-immunoglobulin-like domain adhesion receptor, was expressed by both hypodermal cells and melanophores.
evidence: Stated as a result of the analysis.

claim: Jam3b mediates homophilic and heterophilic adhesive interactions, and is required autonomously by melanophores for an adherent phenotype.
source: Jam3b mediates homophilic and heterophilic adhesive interactions, and is required autonomously by melanophores for an adherent phenotype; a Jam3b fusion protein accumulates at sites of overlap between mature melanophores (Ebnet, 2017; Eom et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature.

claim: In the absence of Jam3b, melanophores tend to be hypopigmented, fail to acquire their mature, well-spread morphology and orderly arrangement, and many die.
source: In the absence of Jam3b, melanophores tend to be hypopigmented, fail to acquire their mature, well-spread morphology and orderly arrangement, and many die.
evidence: Stated as a known consequence of Jam3b loss.

claim: Jam3b facilitates interactions between immature melanophores and hypodermis, with subsequent Jam3b-mediated interactions between melanophores facilitating Kitlga-dependent maturation and survival.
source: Together with prior studies, our observations suggest a model in which Jam3b facilitates interactions between immature melanophores and hypodermis, with subsequent Jam3b-mediated interactions between melanophores facilitating Kitlga-dependent maturation and survival (Figure 8H).
evidence: Inferred from the results and shown in Figure 8H.

claim: asip2b was expressed by xanthophores.
source: That a second factor likely repressive for melanogenesis, asip2b, was expressed by xanthophores further suggests a mechanism for preventing differentiation of new melanophores within the interstripe.
evidence: Stated as a result of the analysis.

claim: Hypodermal cells are the presumptive major source of Csf1b.
source: Our sci-RNA-seq dataset shows hypodermal cells to be the presumptive major source of Csf1b, though its transcripts were detected at lower levels in other dermal mesenchyme, superficial pre-SFCs, and other cell types as well (Figure 8F–H, Figure 8—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Stated as a result of the analysis and shown in figures.

claim: Fish homozygous for csf1a mutations had overtly normal pigment patterns on the trunk but less regular patterns of pigment cells on the fins.
source: As late juveniles (~16 SSL), fish homozygous for csf1a mutations had overtly normal pigment patterns on the trunk but less regular patterns of pigment cells on the fins as compared to wild-type (Figure 8—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Stated as a result of examining mutant fish and shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 2.

claim: Fish homozygous for a csf1b mutation were deficient for pigmented xanthophores, evident particularly on the dorsum.
source: By contrast, fish homozygous for a csf1b mutation were deficient for pigmented xanthophores, evident particularly on the dorsum, which lacks csf1a-expressing iridophores in the hypodermis, though some xanthophores persisted along scale margins where a few iridophores occur (e.g. Supplementary Figure 4 of Guzman et al., 2013).
evidence: Stated as a result of examining mutant fish with citation and shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 2.

claim: Fish doubly homozygous for csf1a and csf1b mutations lacked virtually all xanthophores, recapitulating the phenotype of csf1ra mutants.
source: Fish doubly homozygous for csf1a and csf1b mutations lacked virtually all xanthophores, recapitulating the phenotype of csf1ra mutants.
evidence: Stated as a result of examining mutant fish and shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 2.

claim: Hypodermally derived Csf1b promotes xanthophore differentiation during normal development, and can substitute for iridophore-derived Csf1a in backgrounds deficient for iridophores.
source: These observations support a model in which hypodermally derived Csf1b promotes xanthophore differentiation during normal development, and can substitute for iridophore-derived Csf1a in backgrounds deficient for iridophores; we presume that eventual recovery of xanthophores in bnc2 mutants deficient for both iridophores and hypodermis reflects residual Csf1b availability from other dermal cell types.
evidence: Inferred from the results of the mutant analysis.

claim: More differentially expressed genes were found in iridophores than xanthophores or melanophores in bnc2 mutants.
source: Consistent with this idea and a greater impact of bnc2 loss on iridophores than other pigment cells, we found more differentially expressed genes in iridophores than xanthophores or melanophores (~1000 cells of each cell type) (Figure 8—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Stated as a result of the analysis and shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Iridophores express bnc2 at levels greater than melanophores or xanthophores.
source: Alternatively, bnc2 may have more pronounced activities within iridophores, as these cells express bnc2 and at levels greater than melanophores or xanthophores (Figure 8F), in addition to its non-autonomous functions in pattern formation through the hypodermis (Lang et al., 2009).
evidence: Stated as a result of the analysis with citation and shown in Figure 8F.

claim: Hypodermal cells are a key source of factors permissive, and possibly instructive, for adult interstripe and stripe development.
source: Though further manipulative analyses will be needed to test these several interactions, our analyses of gene expression and cell type abundance identify hypodermal cells as a key source of factors permissive, and possibly instructive, for adult interstripe and stripe development.
evidence: Inferred from the analyses of gene expression and cell type abundance.
